Question: When can I retire as an expat, and what are the biggest expat retirement mistakes?
Answer: When you can retire as an expat depends on how much you have now, how much you need, and what you are investing in. If you have a mixed portfolio of stocks and bonds, you can withdraw 3%- 4% per year, depending on how long you want your retirement to last. (Source, Quora and MyMoneyDesign). If you are in cash, you can’t withdraw more than 3%, as inflation will erode the money. So, having too much money in cash is the first mistake. Apart from that, the three biggest mistakes are: 1. Not factoring in currency risks When I started travelling in 2007, the Pound was 2:1 against the USD, and many British ex-pats relied on that to last forever, which it didn't. The South African Rand and many currencies have fared far worse. This especially affects expats who have a specific income. 2. Not factoring in indirect costs like the hassles of owning certain assets If you rely on rental income as an expat, you face the previous risk - currency risks. What you might not be factoring in is hassles. As a 75-year-old, do you want to chase up tenants to pay? 3. Tax risks and complexity Linked to the second point, having numerous assets, such as properties in many locations, can be a hassle. It can also increase tax risks and complexity. Depending on your situation, a simpler solution can often make sense, like owning one house and having one or two simple portfolios.

Question: What are essential life lessons children are not taught in school?
Answer: One of the easiest ways is how you teach kids when they say “it isn’t fair”. One of the best-suggested responses I have heard for this is - “life isn’t fair. If it were, you yourself probably wouldn't have it so good!”. It isn’t just children either. Many people don’t grow out of this idea that life should be fair. We see it in the way people speak. They overestimate their ideas rather than focusing on execution. They think the market, which means people's decisions, cares about them. This is called the spotlight effect. The world and markets aren’t fair, and people are focusing less on you than you ever imagined. Chance, randomness, and luck play significant roles in success, and hard work alone is no guarantee of success. So, once we accept all these realities, we start to understand some factors that can lead to success that we weren’t taught at school. For example, one of the biggest ways people can become more successful is by taking advantage of luck and coming back from adversity. A simple example: Winning the lottery is pure luck, but how many people take advantage of that good fortune to create generational wealth? Very few. Footballers started to get paid big money in the 1990s and 2000s. Hardly anybody took full advantage of it, but Robbie Fowler created a vast property portfolio by also taking advantage of the lower interest rates at the time. Buy-to-let is much more difficult in the UK compared to the 1990s and early 2000s. So, he took advantage of two big pieces of luck - an ideal time to be a footballer and a great time to invest in property compared to now. Few others in his situation took full advantage. So, teaching kids pragmatism and a bit less idealism would be a good start. That doesn’t mean we should be 100% pragmatic and 0% idealistic, but we need a more sensible balance than teaching young people to be very idealistic. It would also create a more peaceful world in some ways. Let’s not forget that idealism and “this isn’t fair” was the biggest cause of hundreds of millions of people dying in the last century. Communism started in an idealistic fashion and ended up killing so many!

Question: How do I escape from asset rich but cash poor?
Answer: I will define cash-poor as meaning “liquidity-poor”. In other words, you don’t hold cash, bonds, stocks, ETFs, and other assets that can easily be sold. So, anyway, to answer your question, the vast majority of asset-rich and cash-poor people have too much: For most people, property and a primary business are the biggest reasons for being asset-rich and cash-poor. This is so common that many people now have a term for this - house poor. Think of old widows in New York and London who bought their properties decades ago. Or business owners who on paper have a lot of wealth, but are worried that something could happen to change that. To answer your question, there are three main ways around this: 1. Liquidate some assets Downsize your house. Sell some of your business to somebody else. 2. Direct more new investments towards liquid investments Let’s say you don’t want to sell some shares of your new business. You can still increase dividends if you have a profitable business, and slightly reduce reinvestments into the company. Indeed, your own business can often be the most profitable investment once you have established yourself. But the risks are higher, the returns depend on your health and you will never get away from being asset-rich/cash-poor unless you pay yourself more dividends and invest elsewhere or sell some of the business. One of the biggest reasons people end up cash-poor at 60 is that they always convinced themselves that it is silly to invest for 6%-10% per annum returns where “I can get more from investing in my business”. One day you have to bite the bullet and accept lower returns for a portion of your wealth in return for more safety. 3. Use insurance or debt if you aren’t keen on options one and two, you might be able to use some of your assets to take out loans and create new cash flow. Be careful with how much leverage you take out, though. Or you can use insurance. Many people are worried about being cash-poor because: Insurance can deal with some of these concerns. Examples include keyman and partnership insurance, disability and life cover. That will help cover any short or medium-term liquidity needs that arise from death or disability before the assets can be sold off.

Question: What's wrong with today's generation?
Answer: Imagine we are in 2050, 2060, 2070 or 2080. Young people now are middle-aged or very old. They get told by the youngsters of the future, “It was OK for you. Inheritances were massive in the 2020s and 2030s because the baby boomers died. Moreover, as they were all retiring during the same period, getting them to hand over their businesses for zero dollars down was easy. That isn’t to mention the potential of AI, which went on to disrupt the world in a massive way”. What’s the problem with that mindset? The problem is that in 2024, it isn’t apparent to most people that all of these things are opportunities. Sure, a small number of people are watching videos like the one below about how to structure deals for retiring baby boomers, but it isn’t an obvious opportunity for most people. (Source: YouTube How to Buy a Business With No Money in 2024) Likewise, countless people have said to me, “It was OK for you. You got into social media before COVID-19, when it was easier.” Well, if it was obvious, why didn’t everybody do it? The same thing is true for the 1990s and the tech bubble. Many people assume it was easy when Google Ads only cost $1 or less, but if that is the case, why didn’t everybody jump on the opportunity? The point is that every single period has threats and opportunities, positives and negatives, that weren't obvious at the time. If they were obvious, everybody would make money from them. So, to answer your question, there is nothing wrong with this generation if you mean younger people in their late teens and early 20s. Most generations probably think they have it tough compared to their parents and grandparents, and, indeed, succeeding using traditional means (going to university, getting a job, retiring at 65 with a full pension from work) is more difficult than before. But some opportunities didn’t exist before. You can now run a global business from your laptop. You can become a digital nomad and take advantage of lower living costs. As the older generation retires and a percentage gets fed up with running their businesses, there are opportunities to buy them out for little to no money and have a deal whereby they get some of the future revenue, as per the above. The problem is that social media has encouraged a kind of victim mentality amongst many people, including younger people. Building wealth requires you to understand some basic truths, such as nobody, including the government, will save you, and it is better to focus on what you can control. Those who see the positives in the current environment will always have an advantage. It reminds me of COVID-19. Some restaurants and cafes cried for government help, whereas others took advantage of the situation with takeouts, social media, and other means. An opportunity is always a threat, and vice versa. Just wait until younger people today start reminiscing about “the good old days”.

Question: What's the most underrated skill or trait that people should cultivate for a successful life?
Answer: Imagine you are health conscious, but you have a few bad habits. You try hard to change them, read a lot and try to depend on self-discipline. Then, you get an awful diagnosis. Question: Is it true that the world's richest are actually off the Forbes list?

That includes the numbers quoted on lists like this and the Sunday Times rich list. I watched an interview with Deborah Meaden a few days ago, a judge on the UK version of Shark Tank (called Dragons Den). She spoke about the delusional valuations many businesspeople place on their business. Beyond that, as she pointed out, lists like the Sunday Times Rich List (and Forbes) are very misleading, based on projections about what these people’s businesses might be worth if they sold out. That can make sense if somebody has a listed business on the stock market, but it is tough to value a private company that isn’t on the stock market. That is why President Trump’s true net worth has become a polarized topic - his opponents say he is exaggerating his net worth, and he (and many of his supporters) say the opposite. Either way, it is almost impossible to say how much The Trump Organization is worth unless it gets sold or goes onto the stock market. That is why liquid net worth - how much somebody has in liquid assets such as ETFs, funds, cash, etc. - is a better indication of how well somebody has done in many cases. Having loads of money in assets that you may never be able to sell isn’t the same thing as actually realizing gains, or knowing you can press the sell button on a liquid asset tomorrow.

On paper there is a huge difference between say Switzerland and some parts of Eastern Europe. Yet Bucharest in Romania looks, in some areas at least, as developed as anywhere else: I wouldn’t base assumptions on development with technology and tall buildings though. Look at Monaco and Switzerland. Two of the richest places in the world by GDP Per Capita, but they look less developed than Shanghai or Beijing to the naked eye. Any government can build loads of tall buildings in the biggest cities.

Question: What aspect of modern life is most overrated?
Answer: Social media. Let me qualify my statement. Social media isn’t overrated when it comes to leveraging it for business or staying in contact with long-time friends who have moved away. However, social media is over-rated as it has made the spotlight effect worse. The spotlike effect, to quote Wikipedia, is “the psychological phenomenon by which people tend to believe they are being noticed more than they really are. Being that one is constantly in the center of one's own world, an accurate evaluation of how much one is noticed by others is uncommon” It is human nature to believe we are being noticed more than we are because this was our experience as kids. Yet many people in business and life don’t put themselves out there because they are afraid of getting noticed, or being laughed at. How many people do you know who didn’t start a YouTube channel, or something else like that, despite it being useful in their business, because they were worried about negative comments and being noticed by friends and family? It is common. Yet people don’t really care. This quote has been accredited to Churchill. Some people say he never said it. Regardless if it is true whoever said it: Apart from some key people, few care about your posts. So, it is better to just actually try to put yourself out there to get what you want. The more traction and attention you get, the more your life will get better, if you are using social media to get a job, improving your network, having a bigger personal brand and growing your business. Using social media for the below is very over-rated. You will just end up broke, with less financial freedom, for no good reason. Picture credits: AZ quotes.

Question: Why is Britain a debt-ridden society and what can be done to resolve the national debt problem?
Answer: The UK government debt isn’t as high as it has sometimes historically been, even though there is a debate about off-balance sheet debt. Household debt is high, but not higher than in many other countries. Ultimately, if a country has most of its debts in the local currency then it doesn’t have to default. I think what could happen is that inflation is used to pay down debt. I don’t mean out-of-control inflation, but even an average of 3%-4% per year inflation versus the 2% target. That would gradually erode debts. It also means that the Pound could keep falling against the USD. People forget that the Pound has been falling against the USD for about a hundred years. That could continue. The why is more complicated, but the obsession with housing doesn’t help. Most British people have mortgage debt rather than using credit cards. If interest rates stay high, house prices will fall.

Question: Is it better to live in Vietnam, Laos or Cambodia?
Answer: I lived in Cambodia many years ago and visited all three. I also have clients, friends and/or associates in all three. Basically, Laos seems like the least developed country out of the three, despite having a GDP per capita higher than Cambodia. The basic living conditions seem more basic, and it is quite sleepy. Cambodia is growing fast, and you can live almost as good a life in Phnom Penh as Singapore if you have the right budget. Vietnam is the most developed of the three, and the easiest to live. Honestly, though, I find expats who claim to dislike developed countries end up going back to them after a period away. I have run out of the number of expats who lived in some of the cheapest and least developed places and then ended up in places like Japan, Hong Kong, South Korea, Singapore and the UAE. Ultimately, there are conveniences associated with living in a more developed place. That isn’t to mention that taxes are often lower in some of these places, which more than makes up for the higher living costs.
